message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This proposal pulls together several independent sources of evidence. Our access-control data show clearly that the clubs have spare daytime capacity, so new members cost us almost nothing to accommodate. A survey of 640 local non-members tells us there is real demand at £29, with identifiable target groups, and our competitors' pricing confirms that £29 sits in the market range. We have also thought about retention, not just acquisition. Our own data show members who attend classes churn at less than half the rate of those who do not, so the extra daytime classes are not a cost so much as an investment in keeping the new members we recruit. The projection is conservative at 300 new members per club, well within what the survey implies, and after fully costing the extra classes it still delivers around £193,000 a year in net revenue. Members who want more can upgrade at any time. I am confident this is a well-targeted, low-risk way to grow the business.
</author>

The review is to check that the recommendation is clear and the document is ready to go to the decision-makers.

<document>
Pricing Proposal: Introducing an Off-Peak Membership
Pulse Fitness, Commercial Team, August 2026

1. Proposal
We propose introducing an off-peak membership at £29 a month from 1 October 2026, alongside our existing standard membership at £42 a month. Off-peak members would have access before 4 pm on weekdays and all day at weekends, with full access to the gym floor and to classes running in those hours.

2. Background
Pulse operates four clubs with 9,600 standard members. Membership has been flat for 18 months, while two budget gyms have opened within our catchments, both offering memberships at £22 to £25 a month. Our clubs are busy between 5 pm and 8 pm on weekdays, when the gym floor often runs at or near capacity, but quiet during weekday daytimes, when typical utilisation is around 30%.

Access-control data for May to July 2026 show that 31% of our current standard members visit exclusively in what would be the off-peak window, and a further 22% visit mostly off-peak.

3. Market evidence
A survey of 640 non-members living within two miles of our clubs, conducted in June, found that 19% would "definitely" or "probably" join at £29 a month for off-peak access. The most interested groups were retirees, shift workers, parents of school-age children and students.

Four of our six closest competitors already offer an off-peak or daytime membership, priced between £25 and £32.

4. Classes and retention
Retention is the other half of our commercial challenge. Monthly churn among members who attend at least one class a week is 2.1%, against 4.8% among members who do not attend classes. Classes clearly keep members loyal, so we will add six extra daytime classes per club each week to support the new membership, which should lower churn among off-peak members towards the 2.1% level. The additional classes would cost £18,700 a month across the four clubs in instructor fees.

5. Revenue projection
We expect to recruit 1,200 new off-peak members in the first year, about 300 per club, which is consistent with the survey response and the size of our catchments. At £29 a month, this is £34,800 a month, or £417,600 a year, in new membership revenue. After the cost of the additional classes (£224,400 a year), net additional revenue is £193,200 a year.

Because daytime utilisation is low, the additional members can be accommodated without investment in equipment or space.

6. Operational changes
Access control will be updated so that off-peak members' cards do not open the turnstiles outside their access window. Off-peak members will have weekday access until 5 pm, giving those finishing early shifts or school pick-ups time to train. Members will be able to upgrade to standard membership at any time, and to switch between membership types with one month's notice.

7. Risks
Some standard members may perceive the off-peak price as unfair. We will communicate the change as an extension of choice. Competitor responses are possible; the budget gyms already price below our proposed off-peak rate, so we do not expect a price war.

8. Staff consultation
Club managers and front-of-house teams at all four clubs were consulted in July. Managers supported the proposal, noting that daytime classes are often under-filled and that a daytime membership would help build a regular community at quieter times. Front-of-house staff asked for clear signage and app messaging about access hours, which we will provide before launch.

9. Recommendation
The off-peak membership fills spare daytime capacity, responds to competitor offers and targets clearly identified customer groups. We project net additional revenue of around £193,000 a year and recommend launch on 1 October 2026.
</document>
response:
# Review: Off-Peak Membership Proposal

**The recommendation is clear, but the document is not ready for decision-makers.** The headline figure of £193,000 net leaves out a cost that, on the document's own data, is larger than the projected gain. There are also inconsistencies a careful reader will spot.

## Critical issues

### 1. Existing members switching down to off-peak is not costed, and it likely reverses the result

Section 2 says 31% of the 9,600 standard members (about 2,976 people) already visit *exclusively* in the off-peak window. Section 6 lets members switch membership type with one month's notice. Each of those members could pay £13 a month less for the same use.

| Scenario | Members switching | Annual revenue lost |
|---|---|---|
| All exclusive off-peak users switch | 2,976 | **£464,000** |
| Half switch | 1,488 | £232,000 |
| A third switch | 992 | £155,000 |

If even half switch, the loss exceeds the £193,200 net gain, and the proposal loses money. The further 22% who visit "mostly off-peak" add more risk. Section 7 treats this only as a *perception* risk ("may perceive the off-peak price as unfair"). The real risk is lost revenue, and it needs to be in the projection.

**Fix:** Model downgrades explicitly with a range of switching rates. Show the break-even switching rate, and consider mitigations such as a minimum term or excluding existing members for a period.

### 2. The access window is defined two different ways

- Section 1: access "before 4 pm on weekdays"
- Section 6: "weekday access until 5 pm"

This matters for two reasons. It changes how many existing members fall inside the window, so the 31% and 22% figures depend on which definition was used. And 5 pm is when Section 2 says the clubs start running "at or near capacity." Choose one definition and state which one the access-control analysis used.

### 3. The launch date has passed

The document is dated August 2026 and recommends launch on 1 October 2026. It is now mid-November. The date and timeline need updating, and any figures tied to that start date should be refreshed.

## Significant issues

### 4. First-year revenue assumes all 1,200 members join on day one

£34,800 × 12 = £417,600 only holds if every new member is paying from month one. Recruitment will build over the year, so first-year revenue will be well below this. New members will also churn. Even at the optimistic 2.1% monthly rate, that is a meaningful loss over a year. Meanwhile the class costs (£224,400) start in full straight away. A month-by-month ramp would give a more honest figure.

### 5. "Conservative" is not supported by the evidence

- The 19% figure is stated intent ("definitely" or "probably"), which typically overstates actual sign-ups by a wide margin.
- The document never gives the catchment population, so readers cannot check that 300 per club is "consistent with" the survey. Show the calculation: catchment population × assumed conversion rate.

### 6. The classes case is internally contradictory and not quantified

- **Contradiction:** Section 8 says managers report that "daytime classes are often under-filled." That makes it hard to justify £224,400 a year for six *more* daytime classes per club. It may be better to fill the existing classes first.
- **Causation:** The 2.1% vs 4.8% churn gap shows that class-goers churn less. It does not show that adding classes *causes* lower churn, since more committed members are likelier both to attend classes and to stay. "Classes clearly keep members loyal" overstates this.
- **Not in the numbers:** The classes are justified on retention grounds, but no retention benefit appears in the projection. Either quantify it or reconsider the cost.

## Minor issues

- **Competitor reasoning (Section 7):** The budget gyms already undercut you, so a price war is unlikely to start with them. The more relevant question is how the four competitors with £25–32 off-peak offers might respond.
- **Arithmetic:** The stated sums are correct (£18,700 × 12 = £224,400; 1,200 × £29 × 12 = £417,600; net £193,200). The problems are in the assumptions, not the calculations.

## On the author's summary

The summary describes the projection as conservative and the proposal as low-risk, and it presents switching only as upgrades ("Members who want more can upgrade at any time"). The bigger exposure is in the other direction: downgrades by existing off-peak users. The proposal may still be worth doing, since there is real spare capacity and competitive pressure. But the case for it needs to survive a downgrade analysis before it goes forward.

## Suggested next steps before circulation

1. Add a cannibalisation model with a break-even switching rate and proposed safeguards.
2. Settle on a single access window and re-check the access data against it.
3. Rebuild the first-year projection with a recruitment ramp and churn.
4. Reconcile the extra-classes proposal with managers' comments on under-filled classes, or cut or phase it.
5. Update the launch date and timeline.
6. Revise the Risks and Recommendation sections to reflect the above.
